tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Day 1, 1400 (Emergency Department → Telemetry): 72-year-old client with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (EF 30% on echo 6 months ago), hypertension, and type 2 diabetes reports 4 days of worsening shortness of breath and leg swelling. States a family holiday meal included ham and canned soup. See admission assessment in the question.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. The nurse completes the admission assessment below. Click to highlight the findings that require follow-up by the nurse.
questions.passage: The client states, "I {{ran out of my water pill 5 days ago}} and didn't want to bother anyone." Reports {{sleeping upright in a recliner for the past 3 nights}}. {{Alert and oriented ×4}}. Respirations labored at rest with {{SpO₂ 89% on room air}}. {{Crackles to the mid-lung fields bilaterally}}. {{Bowel sounds active in all 4 quadrants}}. {{Radial pulses 2+ and equal bilaterally}}. {{3+ pitting edema of both legs to the knees}}. Reports {{chronic arthritis pain in the hands, 2/10}}.
optionRationales: Requires follow-up. Stopping the loop diuretic (plus a high-sodium meal) is the likely trigger for fluid retention and must be addressed in the plan and discharge teaching.
Requires follow-up. Needing to sleep upright is orthopnea — pulmonary congestion from left ventricular failure worsens when lying flat.
Does not require follow-up. Intact orientation is reassuring; confusion would suggest poor cerebral perfusion or hypoxemia.
Requires follow-up. An SpO₂ of 89% on room air is hypoxemia and is the most urgent finding.
Requires follow-up. Crackles extending to the mid-lung fields indicate alveolar fluid from pulmonary congestion.
Does not require follow-up. Active bowel sounds are a normal finding.
Does not require follow-up. Equal 2+ radial pulses indicate adequate peripheral arterial perfusion at this time.
Requires follow-up. Bilateral 3+ pitting edema to the knees reflects systemic venous congestion and fluid volume excess.
Does not require follow-up now. Chronic, mild, stable arthritis pain is not related to the acute problem (and NSAIDs, which worsen HF, should be avoided later).
questions.rationale: Recognizing cues means separating abnormal, relevant data from expected or unrelated data. The missed diuretic, orthopnea, hypoxemia, crackles, and bilateral pitting edema all point to fluid overload with pulmonary and systemic congestion. Orientation, bowel sounds, equal radial pulses, and chronic mild arthritis pain are normal or unrelated to the acute problem.
questions.takeaway: In HF, cluster the cues: missed diuretic + sodium load + orthopnea + crackles + edema + low SpO₂ = decompensation.
questions.hintContent: Recall the findings of left-sided (pulmonary) congestion and right-sided (systemic) congestion, and what typically triggers a heart failure exacerbation.
questions.hintStrategy: Highlight only the findings that are abnormal AND relevant to the client's current problem; normal or chronic, unrelated findings should be left unhighlighted.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Day 1, 1400: 72-year-old client with HFrEF (EF 30%), hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. Ran out of furosemide 5 days ago; ate a high-sodium holiday meal. Sleeping upright for 3 nights. Crackles to mid-lung fields bilaterally, S3 heard at the apex, jugular venous pulsation 8 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, 3+ pitting edema to the knees bilaterally. Alert and oriented ×4.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: The client's findings are most consistent with {0}. The elevated BNP primarily reflects {1}, and the S3 heart sound indicates {2}.

options: acute decompensated heart failure
community-acquired pneumonia
acute coronary syndrome
exacerbation of COPD
myocardial cell death from coronary occlusion
ventricular wall stretch from volume and pressure overload
reduced renal clearance from dehydration
a systemic inflammatory response to infection
a stiff, hypertrophied atrium contracting forcefully
turbulent flow across a narrowed aortic valve
rapid filling into an overloaded, poorly contracting ventricle
friction between inflamed pericardial layers

questions.rationale: Orthopnea, crackles, JVD, bilateral edema, an S3, hypoxemia, and a markedly elevated BNP after a missed diuretic and a sodium load describe acute decompensated heart failure. BNP is released by ventricular myocytes in response to wall stretch from volume/pressure overload. An S3 (ventricular gallop) in an adult with HF reflects rapid early-diastolic filling into a volume-overloaded, poorly compliant ventricle. The normal troponin, absence of fever, and lack of wheezing argue against ACS, pneumonia, and COPD; an S4 comes from atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, and friction rubs come from pericarditis.
questions.takeaway: BNP = ventricular stretch; S3 in an adult with HF = volume overload.
questions.hintContent: Recall which cells release BNP and what stimulus triggers its release, and when in the cardiac cycle an S3 occurs.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the normal troponin, the absence of fever, and the fluid-related cues to rule out the competing conditions before choosing the mechanism blanks.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Day 1, 1430: 72-year-old client with acute decompensated HFrEF. Crackles to mid-lung fields, orthopnea, 3+ bilateral leg edema, skin over shins taut and shiny. Weight 91.2 kg (201 lb); reported dry weight 87.5 kg (193 lb). States, "I don't understand why I need so many pills."

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Which client problem is the nurse's priority at this time?
options: Risk for skin breakdown related to edematous, taut skin of the lower legs
Knowledge deficit related to the purpose of the prescribed medication regimen
Impaired gas exchange related to fluid accumulation in the alveoli
Electrolyte imbalance related to dilutional hyponatremia
optionRationales: Edematous skin is at risk for breakdown, but this is a potential problem and does not threaten life as quickly as hypoxemia.
Teaching is essential before discharge, but a client who is hypoxemic and dyspneic cannot learn effectively; this is addressed once the client is stable.
Correct. Pulmonary congestion is impairing oxygenation (SpO₂ falling from 89% to 88%, RR 28). Breathing/oxygenation is the actual, acute, life-threatening problem.
A sodium of 132 mEq/L is mildly low from fluid retention and needs monitoring, but it is not causing symptoms and is less urgent than hypoxemia.
questions.rationale: Using ABCs and 'actual over potential,' the priority is the problem that threatens oxygenation. The falling SpO₂, tachypnea, and crackles show fluid in the alveoli impairing gas exchange. Skin risk and knowledge deficit are real but less urgent, and mild dilutional hyponatremia is asymptomatic.
questions.takeaway: Hypoxemia from pulmonary congestion outranks skin, teaching, and mild lab changes.
questions.hintContent: Recall how fluid in the alveoli affects diffusion of oxygen and which trends in the vital signs show the problem is worsening.
questions.hintStrategy: Apply ABCs and 'actual before potential.' Ask which problem, if unaddressed in the next hour, is most likely to harm the client.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Day 1, 1445: Acute decompensated HFrEF. Crackles to mid-lung fields, orthopnea, SpO₂ 88% on room air, HR 110, BP 160/92, 3+ bilateral leg edema. Urine output 30 mL/hr.

tabs.title: Orders
tabs.html:
• Oxygen via nasal cannula; titrate to SpO₂ 92–96%
  • Furosemide 40 mg IV push now, then 40 mg IV every 12 hours
  • Sodium-restricted (2 g) diet; fluid restriction 1,500 mL/24 hr
  • Daily weight; strict intake and output
  • Continuous telemetry
  • Basic metabolic panel in the morning

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes and Orders. For each potential nursing intervention, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated for the client at this time.
rows: Position the client in high Fowler's position with legs dependent
Administer a 500-mL 0.9% sodium chloride bolus for the heart rate of 110
Weigh the client each morning before breakfast using the same scale
Encourage 3 L of oral fluid daily to protect the kidneys during diuresis
Titrate oxygen to keep SpO₂ within the prescribed range
optionRationales: Indicated. Upright positioning with legs down reduces venous return (preload) and lets the diaphragm descend, easing dyspnea.
Contraindicated. The tachycardia is compensatory for low cardiac output and hypoxemia, not hypovolemia; a saline bolus would worsen pulmonary congestion.
Indicated. A consistent daily weight (same time, scale, and clothing, after voiding) is the best indicator of fluid balance and diuretic response.
Contraindicated. The client is fluid overloaded with a 1,500 mL/day restriction; forcing fluids would worsen congestion.
Indicated. Supplemental oxygen treats hypoxemia; titrating to the prescribed target avoids both under- and over-oxygenation.
questions.rationale: Solutions for acute decompensated HF reduce preload and congestion (upright positioning, diuresis, sodium and fluid restriction), support oxygenation, and monitor response (daily weights, I&O). Fluid boluses and liberal fluid intake add volume to an already overloaded circulation.
questions.takeaway: In fluid-overloaded HF: sit up, legs down, O₂, diuretic, restrict sodium/fluid, weigh daily — no fluid boluses.
questions.hintContent: Recall how preload affects a failing ventricle and why tachycardia can be compensatory in low cardiac output.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each row independently: ask whether the intervention removes volume/improves oxygenation (indicated) or adds volume to an overloaded circulation (contraindicated).

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Day 1, 2000: Received furosemide 40 mg IV at 1450. Urine output since 1450: 1,650 mL. Breathing easier; crackles now in bases only. SpO₂ 94% on 2 L/min nasal cannula. Client reports leg cramps. Telemetry shows sinus rhythm at 96/min with new occasional premature ventricular contractions (PVCs).

tabs.title: Orders
tabs.html:
• Potassium replacement protocol: K⁺ 3.0–3.4 mEq/L → potassium chloride 40 mEq PO once; recheck K⁺ 4 hours after dose
  • Furosemide 40 mg IV every 12 hours (next dose 0250)
  • Continuous telemetry

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Laboratory Results, and Orders. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Administer potassium chloride 40 mEq by mouth per the replacement protocol
Notify the provider of the potassium level and the new PVCs
Administer potassium chloride 20 mEq by IV push to correct the level quickly
Cancel the 0250 furosemide dose because the client has diuresed well
Continue telemetry monitoring and observe for increasing ventricular ectopy
Encourage the client to drink extra water to replace the urine output
optionRationales: Correct. The level falls within the protocol range; giving the prescribed oral replacement corrects the diuretic-induced hypokalemia.
Correct. New ventricular ectopy with hypokalemia is a change in condition that the provider should know about, even while the protocol is initiated.
Incorrect. Potassium is never given by IV push — it can cause fatal dysrhythmias or cardiac arrest. IV potassium must be diluted and infused by pump.
Incorrect. The nurse cannot discontinue a prescribed medication independently; the client still has crackles and edema. Concerns are discussed with the provider.
Correct. Hypokalemia increases ventricular irritability; continuous monitoring allows early recognition of worsening dysrhythmias.
Incorrect. The client remains fluid overloaded with a 1,500 mL restriction; diuresis is the therapeutic goal, not something to replace.
questions.rationale: Loop diuretics cause potassium loss, and hypokalemia increases ventricular irritability (PVCs, leg cramps). The nurse implements the replacement protocol, notifies the provider of the new ectopy, and continues telemetry. IV push potassium is lethal, the nurse cannot independently cancel the diuretic, and replacing diuresed volume defeats the treatment goal.
questions.takeaway: Loop diuretic → K⁺ loss → PVCs/cramps: replace per protocol, monitor rhythm, never give K⁺ IV push.
questions.hintContent: Recall which electrolyte loop diuretics waste, what low levels do to cardiac muscle, and the safety rules for potassium administration.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option as true/false on its own. Eliminate any option that is unsafe or outside the nurse's independent scope.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Day 3, 0800: Lungs with faint crackles in the bases only; sleeping on 1 pillow. Leg edema 1+ at the ankles. SpO₂ 95% on room air. When assisted to stand for the morning weight, the client reports feeling lightheaded; BP lying 128/76, HR 80 → standing (1 min) 104/66, HR 102. Weight 88.6 kg (195.3 lb), down from 91.2 kg (201 lb) on admission.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes and Laboratory Results. For each finding on day 3, indicate whether it shows the client's condition is improving or requires follow-up.
rows: Weight decreased 2.6 kg (5.7 lb) since admission
Crackles limited to the bases; sleeping on 1 pillow
Standing BP 104/66 with HR 102 and lightheadedness
Serum creatinine increased from 1.4 to 1.9 mg/dL
optionRationales: Improving. About 1 kg equals 1 L of fluid; losing 2.6 kg shows effective diuresis toward the client's dry weight.
Improving. Less pulmonary congestion and resolution of orthopnea show better left ventricular unloading.
Requires follow-up. A 24 mm Hg systolic drop with symptoms meets orthostatic hypotension criteria and suggests over-diuresis — a fall risk.
Requires follow-up. A rising creatinine (with BUN 44) suggests reduced renal perfusion from aggressive diuresis; the provider may adjust the diuretic dose.
Improving. Potassium is now within normal limits after replacement.
questions.rationale: Evaluating outcomes compares current data with goals. Weight loss, clearing lungs, resolved orthopnea, falling BNP, and normal potassium show the treatment is working. However, symptomatic orthostatic hypotension and a rising BUN/creatinine suggest intravascular depletion and reduced kidney perfusion from diuresis — both need to be reported so therapy can be adjusted and falls prevented.
questions.takeaway: Successful diuresis can overshoot: watch for orthostatic hypotension and rising creatinine.
questions.hintContent: Recall the criteria for orthostatic hypotension and what a rising BUN and creatinine indicate about kidney perfusion.
questions.hintStrategy: For each row, compare the day 3 value with the day 1 value and the goal of therapy; a finding can be a new problem even when the original problem is improving.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: 1015: 78-year-old client with atrial fibrillation admitted yesterday for pneumonia. Reports stopping apixaban 1 week ago "because it cost too much." At 0930 client suddenly developed severe pain in the right lower leg, rated 9/10. Right foot and leg pale and cool to mid-calf; no palpable popliteal, dorsalis pedis, or posterior tibial pulses on the right; no Doppler signal over the right dorsalis pedis. Capillary refill of right toes >5 seconds. Reports numbness of the right toes and can barely wiggle them. Left leg warm and pink with 2+ pulses.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes and Vital Signs. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take to address that condition, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess the client's progress.

options: Deep vein thrombosis
Acute arterial occlusion
Acute compartment syndrome
Chronic venous insufficiency
Elevate the right leg on 2 pillows above heart level
Apply a heating pad to the right foot
Notify the provider immediately using SBAR
Administer the prescribed IV heparin bolus and infusion
Massage the calf gently to stimulate circulation
Calf circumference compared with the left leg
Hemoglobin A1C
Doppler pulse signals, color, and temperature of the right foot
Sensation and movement of the right toes
Orthostatic blood pressure

condition: Incorrect. DVT causes a warm, swollen, often reddened leg with intact arterial pulses — not a pale, cool, pulseless limb.

Correct. Sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia (coolness), paresthesia, and early paralysis in a client with atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation indicate an embolic arterial occlusion.
Incorrect. Compartment syndrome follows trauma, fracture, or reperfusion and usually has a tense compartment with pulses present until late.
Incorrect. Chronic venous insufficiency develops slowly with edema, brown discoloration, and warm skin — not a sudden pulseless limb.
actions: Incorrect. Elevating an ischemic limb further reduces arterial inflow; the leg should be kept flat or slightly dependent.
Incorrect. An ischemic, numb limb cannot sense heat and cannot dissipate it — direct heat risks burns and raises tissue oxygen demand.
Correct. Acute limb ischemia is a vascular emergency; limb viability depends on revascularization within hours.
Correct. Immediate anticoagulation with IV unfractionated heparin prevents clot propagation while revascularization is planned.
Incorrect. Massage does not restore arterial flow and could dislodge thrombus; it has no role here.
parameters: Incorrect. Calf circumference monitors swelling from DVT, not arterial perfusion.
Incorrect. A1C reflects glucose control over about 3 months and does not track acute limb perfusion.
Correct. Return of Doppler signals, warmth, and color shows restored arterial inflow.
Correct. Sensory and motor function reflect nerve and muscle viability; worsening paralysis signals an immediately threatened limb.
Incorrect. Orthostatic BP assesses volume status, not perfusion of the affected limb.

questions.rationale: The '6 Ps' (pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paresthesia, paralysis) in a client with atrial fibrillation who stopped anticoagulation indicate acute embolic arterial occlusion. The nurse notifies the provider immediately and starts prescribed heparin, keeps the limb level or slightly dependent, and avoids heat and elevation. Serial neurovascular checks (pulses by Doppler, color, temperature, sensation, and movement) show whether perfusion is restored.
questions.takeaway: Pale, cold, pulseless, numb limb = arterial emergency: call now, heparin, no elevation, no heat.
questions.hintContent: Recall the '6 Ps' of acute limb ischemia and why atrial fibrillation without anticoagulation matters.
questions.hintStrategy: Pick the condition first, then choose only actions and parameters that fit THAT condition. Watch for options that belong to a venous problem.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: 0630: 81-year-old client admitted 2 days ago from a long-term care facility with a urinary tract infection; oral antibiotic started yesterday. Now newly confused and pulling at bedding. Skin warm and flushed. Indwelling urinary catheter draining 45 mL of cloudy, foul-smelling urine over the past 3 hours. Lungs clear. No JVD. Weight 60 kg (132 lb).

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take to address that condition, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess the client's progress.

options: Cardiogenic shock
Anaphylactic shock
Hypovolemic shock
Septic shock
Administer furosemide to increase urine output
Obtain blood cultures, then start the prescribed IV broad-spectrum antibiotic
Administer the prescribed IV crystalloid bolus of 30 mL/kg
Restrict fluids to 1,000 mL/day to prevent pulmonary edema
Remove the indwelling catheter and obtain a clean-catch specimen
Mean arterial pressure
Serum cholesterol
Serum lactate trend
B-type natriuretic peptide
Peak expiratory flow

condition: Incorrect. Cardiogenic shock presents with cool, clammy skin, crackles, JVD, and an elevated BNP — this client has clear lungs, no JVD, and a normal BNP.
Incorrect. Anaphylaxis follows an allergen exposure with urticaria, angioedema, or wheezing; none are present.
Incorrect. Hypovolemic shock usually causes cool, pale skin and has no fever or leukocytosis; this client's warm skin, fever, and infection source point elsewhere.
Correct. A known infection with fever, leukocytosis, hypotension (MAP 59), lactate >4 mmol/L, new confusion, and oliguria indicate septic shock.
actions: Incorrect. Oliguria here reflects hypoperfusion; a diuretic would worsen hypotension.
Correct. Cultures before antibiotics identify the organism, and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics should begin as soon as possible (ideally within 1 hour of recognition).

Correct. Surviving Sepsis guidance supports at least 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid within the first 3 hours for hypotension or lactate ≥4 mmol/L (1,800 mL for this 60-kg client), with reassessment for fluid overload.
Incorrect. The client is intravascularly depleted from vasodilation and capillary leak; restricting fluid worsens perfusion.
Incorrect. The catheter may need to be replaced, but this is not a priority action for shock and a clean-catch specimen is not possible in a confused client.
parameters: Correct. The target MAP is ≥65 mm Hg; MAP shows whether fluids (and vasopressors, if needed) are restoring perfusion pressure.
Incorrect. Cholesterol has no role in acute sepsis monitoring.
Correct. A falling lactate shows improving tissue perfusion; guidelines recommend remeasuring an elevated initial lactate.
Incorrect. BNP is used to evaluate heart failure, not the response to sepsis resuscitation.
Incorrect. Peak flow monitors airway obstruction in asthma.

questions.rationale: Infection plus hypotension (MAP 59 mm Hg), a lactate of 4.6 mmol/L, altered mentation, and oliguria indicate septic shock — widespread vasodilation and capillary leak cause distributive shock. Initial actions are cultures, prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics, and a crystalloid bolus of 30 mL/kg as prescribed; vasopressors are added if MAP stays below 65 mm Hg despite fluids. Progress is tracked with MAP (goal ≥65 mm Hg), lactate clearance, urine output, and mental status.
questions.takeaway: Sepsis bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressors for MAP <65.
questions.hintContent: Recall how warm skin, fever, and a normal BNP help distinguish distributive shock from cardiogenic and hypovolemic shock.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the condition from the whole picture, then select actions that treat its cause and parameters that measure perfusion — not tests for other body systems.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure · Home Monitoring
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A client with stage 2 hypertension was taught home blood pressure monitoring 2 weeks ago. At the follow-up visit, the client describes the routine below. Click to highlight the practices that indicate the need for further teaching.
questions.passage: "I check my blood pressure {{right after my morning coffee and cigarette}}. I sit at the kitchen table {{with my back supported against the chair}} and {{my feet flat on the floor}}. I rest {{my arm on the table so the cuff is at heart level}}. I wrap {{the cuff over my thin pajama sleeve}}, and I usually {{talk on the phone with my daughter while it inflates}}. I {{take two readings 1 minute apart}} using {{the upper-arm cuff the pharmacist checked for size}}, and I {{write down only the lower reading to show my provider}}."
optionRationales: Needs further teaching. Caffeine and nicotine raise BP; avoid them (and exercise) for at least 30 minutes before measuring.
Correct practice. A supported back prevents isometric muscle contraction that raises BP.
Correct practice. Feet flat and legs uncrossed avoid falsely elevated readings.
Correct practice. An arm supported at heart level avoids falsely high (arm too low) or falsely low (arm too high) readings.
Needs further teaching. The cuff must be placed on bare skin; clothing under the cuff can distort the reading.
Needs further teaching. Talking raises readings; the client should sit quietly during measurement.
Correct practice. The AHA recommends at least two readings 1 minute apart, morning and evening.
Correct practice. A validated upper-arm device with the correct cuff size is recommended.
Needs further teaching. All readings should be recorded (or the device memory shared); reporting only the lower reading hides true BP control.
questions.rationale: Home BP readings guide diagnosis and medication titration, so technique errors can lead to over- or under-treatment. The client should avoid caffeine, smoking, and exercise for 30 minutes, rest quietly 5 minutes, place the cuff on bare skin, stay silent, and record all readings. Sitting with back supported, feet flat, arm at heart level, two readings 1 minute apart, and a validated, properly sized upper-arm cuff are correct.
questions.takeaway: Home BP: no caffeine/smoke 30 min, rest 5 min, bare arm at heart level, silent, 2 readings, record all.
questions.hintContent: Recall the AHA preparation and positioning steps for accurate home BP measurement.
questions.hintStrategy: You are looking for errors. Read each highlighted phrase and ask, 'Would this make the reading inaccurate or misleading?'

questions.stem: Refer to the Vital Signs. The nurse is caring for a client 8 hours after an open abdominal colon resection and documents the assessment below. Click to highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.passage: Client is {{restless and repeatedly asking what time it is}}. Skin {{cool, pale, and moist}}. Heart rate {{118/min, up from 84 at 1400}}. BP {{104/88}}. Temperature {{37.3 °C (99.1 °F)}}. {{SpO₂ 96% on room air}}. Urine output {{60 mL over the past 3 hours}}. Incisional pain {{rated 4/10 after oral oxycodone}}. Abdominal dressing {{dry and intact}}. Bowel sounds {{hypoactive}}.
optionRationales: Requires follow-up. Restlessness and anxiety are early signs of reduced cerebral perfusion in shock.
Requires follow-up. Cool, pale, moist skin reflects sympathetic vasoconstriction shunting blood to vital organs.
Requires follow-up. A rising heart rate is an early compensatory response to falling stroke volume.
Requires follow-up. The systolic BP has fallen and the pulse pressure has narrowed to 16 mm Hg (from 52), indicating reduced stroke volume with vasoconstriction.
Does not require immediate follow-up. A low-grade temperature is common after surgery and does not explain these changes.
Does not require immediate follow-up. Oxygen saturation is within normal limits.
Requires follow-up. Output of 20 mL/hr is below the minimum of 0.5 mL/kg/hr (about 30 mL/hr) and reflects reduced renal perfusion.
Does not require immediate follow-up. Pain controlled to 4/10 is acceptable; uncontrolled pain would be a concern.
Does not require immediate follow-up by itself. A dry dressing does not rule out internal (intra-abdominal) bleeding.
Does not require immediate follow-up. Hypoactive bowel sounds are expected after bowel surgery.
questions.rationale: Early (compensated) hypovolemic shock produces restlessness, tachycardia, cool clammy skin, narrowing pulse pressure, and oliguria before the systolic BP drops dramatically. A dry dressing does not exclude internal hemorrhage after abdominal surgery. Low-grade temperature, controlled pain, normal SpO₂, and hypoactive bowel sounds are expected postoperative findings.
questions.takeaway: Narrowing pulse pressure + rising HR + restlessness + oliguria = compensated shock, even with a 'normal' systolic BP.
questions.hintContent: Recall the compensatory mechanisms (sympathetic activation, vasoconstriction, renal conservation) of early shock and how they change pulse pressure.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare each finding with the 1400 baseline and with expected postoperative findings; highlight changes that signal reduced perfusion.
