questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a 70-year-old client with long-standing peripheral artery disease (PAD), type 2 diabetes, and a 45-pack-year smoking history at a routine clinic visit. Click to highlight the findings that indicate progression of the disease and require prompt follow-up.
questions.passage: Client reports {{calf cramping after walking 2 blocks that resolves with 5 minutes of rest}}, unchanged for a year. New this month: {{burning pain in the right foot at night that is relieved by hanging the leg over the side of the bed}}. On inspection, {{shiny, hairless skin on both lower legs}}, {{thick, slow-growing toenails}}, {{a black, dry area on the tip of the right second toe}}, and {{a pale, punched-out wound on the right lateral ankle that has not healed in 6 weeks}}. {{Dorsalis pedis pulses 1+ bilaterally, unchanged from the last visit}}. {{BP 136/82}}.
optionRationales: Stable. Reproducible claudication that resolves with rest and is unchanged over a year is the expected chronic pattern.
Requires prompt follow-up. Ischemic rest pain relieved by dependency means blood flow is inadequate even at rest — a sign of chronic limb-threatening ischemia.
Expected. Thin, shiny, hairless skin is a chronic trophic change of arterial insufficiency.
Expected. Thickened nails are a chronic trophic change of reduced arterial flow.
Requires prompt follow-up. A black, dry area indicates dry gangrene (tissue necrosis).
Requires prompt follow-up. A nonhealing arterial ulcer (pale base, punched-out edges, lateral ankle) signals critical ischemia and high amputation risk.
Stable. Diminished pulses are expected with PAD; they are unchanged from baseline.
Stable. The BP is stage 1 range and needs ongoing management, but it does not signal limb-threatening progression.
questions.rationale: Chronic PAD commonly causes stable claudication, diminished pulses, and trophic changes (shiny hairless skin, thick nails). Progression to chronic limb-threatening ischemia is signaled by ischemic rest pain (often relieved by dangling the leg), nonhealing wounds, and gangrene — these warrant urgent vascular referral for revascularization evaluation.
questions.takeaway: Claudication is chronic; rest pain, nonhealing wounds, or gangrene = limb-threatening ischemia.
questions.hintContent: Recall the difference between intermittent claudication and ischemic rest pain, and the signs of tissue loss in PAD.
questions.hintStrategy: The stem says 'progression' — distinguish findings that are new or signal tissue death from findings that are expected and stable in chronic PAD.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure · Alternate Sites
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who has short arm casts on both forearms after a fall and a PICC line in the right upper arm. The client's blood pressure must be measured. Which technique should the nurse use?
options: Place a standard adult arm cuff around the lower thigh and auscultate over the popliteal artery
Place the arm cuff on the left upper arm above the cast and auscultate over the brachial artery
Place a thigh cuff on the midthigh with the client prone and auscultate the popliteal artery
Place a thigh-sized cuff on the thigh and expect the systolic reading to be lower than a reading taken on the arm
optionRationales: Incorrect. An arm cuff is too small for the thigh; a cuff that is too small or narrow gives a falsely high reading.
Incorrect. BP should not be measured on a limb with a cast or bulky bandage, even above it.

Correct. With both arms unavailable, the thigh is the alternative site: a large thigh cuff is placed on the midthigh and the popliteal artery is auscultated with the client prone (or supine with the knee slightly flexed).
Incorrect. In adults the thigh systolic pressure is normally about 10–40 mm Hg HIGHER than the brachial pressure; the diastolic is about the same.
questions.rationale: BP is not measured on a limb with a cast, IV/PICC, AV fistula, injury, or on the side of an axillary node dissection. The thigh is the alternate site, using an appropriately sized thigh cuff over the popliteal artery. Thigh systolic readings normally run 10–40 mm Hg higher than brachial readings, so the site must be documented.
questions.takeaway: Thigh BP: large thigh cuff, popliteal artery, systolic runs higher — document the site.
questions.hintContent: Recall which limbs should not be used for BP and how cuff size and the thigh site affect the reading.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that use a restricted limb or the wrong cuff, then check the remaining options for an incorrect expected value.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure · Out-of-Office Measurement
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 48-year-old client has had clinic BP readings of 152/94 and 150/92 at two visits. The client brings a 2-week log from a validated upper-arm home monitor (checked against the clinic device) showing an average of 122/76. The client takes no medications and has no target-organ damage. How should the nurse interpret these data?
options: The client has stage 2 hypertension and needs medication started today
The pattern suggests white-coat hypertension; confirm it with out-of-office monitoring
The pattern suggests masked hypertension, which carries a higher risk than office readings indicate
The home readings are unreliable, so the diagnosis should be based on clinic readings only
optionRationales: Incorrect. Current AHA/ACC guidance recommends confirming an office diagnosis with out-of-office readings; these home readings are normal.

Correct. Elevated office BP (≥130/80) with normal out-of-office BP (<130/80) defines white-coat hypertension; ambulatory or continued home monitoring confirms it, and the client needs periodic follow-up because risk of sustained hypertension is higher.
Incorrect. Masked hypertension is the reverse pattern — normal office readings with elevated out-of-office readings.
Incorrect. A validated upper-arm device checked against the clinic device provides reliable data that guidelines encourage using.
questions.rationale: The AHA/ACC guidelines recommend out-of-office BP (home or ambulatory monitoring) to confirm hypertension and detect white-coat and masked patterns. Office readings ≥130/80 with home averages <130/80 indicate white-coat hypertension. Treating based on office readings alone could lead to unnecessary medication and hypotension at home.
questions.takeaway: High in clinic, normal at home = white-coat; normal in clinic, high at home = masked.
questions.hintContent: Recall how office and out-of-office BP patterns are used to classify white-coat and masked hypertension.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare where the BP is high versus where it is normal, and consider how reliable the home data are before deciding.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure · Severe Hypertension
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 58-year-old client with hypertension ran out of amlodipine 1 week ago. At a clinic visit, the BP is 188/122; after 5 minutes of quiet rest, it is 186/120. The client denies headache, chest pain, dyspnea, vision changes, or weakness, and a focused neurologic exam is normal. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Arrange immediate transfer to the emergency department for an IV antihypertensive infusion
Administer a sublingual immediate-release nifedipine capsule to lower the BP quickly
Have the client lie down in a dark room and recheck the BP in 1 hour before notifying anyone
Notify the provider and anticipate restarting oral therapy with close follow-up
optionRationales: Incorrect. Without acute target-organ damage, severe hypertension does not require emergency IV therapy; rapid lowering can cause cerebral, renal, or coronary ischemia.
Incorrect. Sublingual immediate-release nifedipine causes unpredictable, precipitous BP drops and is not recommended.
Incorrect. The provider should be informed now; delaying communication of a severely elevated BP is unsafe even when the client is asymptomatic.
Correct. BP >180/120 without signs of acute target-organ damage (severe hypertension) is managed by reinstituting or intensifying oral medication with close follow-up.
questions.rationale: The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline defines severe hypertension as BP >180/120. The key question is whether acute target-organ damage is present: if yes, it is a hypertensive emergency needing ICU-level IV therapy; if no, as here, oral therapy is restarted or intensified and BP is lowered gradually over days to weeks. Rapid lowering in an asymptomatic client can cause harm.
questions.takeaway: Severe BP without organ damage → oral meds and follow-up; with organ damage → emergency IV therapy.
questions.hintContent: Recall what distinguishes a hypertensive emergency from severe hypertension without target-organ damage.
questions.hintStrategy: Look at the symptom data in the stem before reacting to the number; the treatment setting depends on whether organs are being damaged.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure · Antihypertensive Therapy · Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 29-year-old client with chronic hypertension that is well controlled on lisinopril 20 mg daily tells the clinic nurse, "My partner and I plan to start trying for a baby next month." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: "Stop the lisinopril now so it is out of your system before you conceive."
"Keep taking it until your pregnancy test is positive, and then stop it."
"Let's arrange a visit with your provider to change medications first."
"Lisinopril is safe in pregnancy, so continue your usual daily dose."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Stopping an antihypertensive without a replacement can cause uncontrolled hypertension; changes are made with the provider.
Incorrect. Waiting until pregnancy is confirmed risks fetal exposure; the regimen should be changed before conception.

Correct. ACE inhibitors (and ARBs) are fetotoxic, causing fetal kidney damage and oligohydramnios. The provider should switch to a pregnancy-compatible agent such as labetalol or nifedipine before conception.
Incorrect. ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy.
questions.rationale: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy because they impair fetal kidney development and can cause oligohydramnios, growth restriction, and fetal death, particularly in the second and third trimesters. Clients of childbearing potential who plan pregnancy should be switched to a pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive (labetalol, nifedipine, or methyldopa) before conception, under provider direction, with continued BP monitoring.
questions.takeaway: Planning pregnancy on an ACE inhibitor or ARB → switch drugs with the provider before conception; never just stop.
questions.hintContent: Recall the pregnancy risk of drugs that block the renin–angiotensin system and which antihypertensives are preferred in pregnancy.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the response that protects both the fetus and the client's BP control while staying within the nurse's scope.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure · Lifespan: Pregnancy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client at 32 weeks' gestation with preeclampsia has a BP of 164/112 that is 166/110 when repeated 15 minutes later. She reports a headache. The provider prescribes labetalol 20 mg IV. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Recheck the BP in 4 hours to confirm the reading before giving any antihypertensive
Give the labetalol within 30–60 minutes of the confirmed severe-range reading
Give the labetalol and titrate further doses to reach a BP below 120/80
Place the client supine and flat to improve blood flow to the placenta
optionRationales: Incorrect. The 4-hour interval is used to diagnose gestational hypertension at 140/90; persistent severe-range BP (≥160/110) is an emergency that must be treated promptly.

Correct. Acute-onset severe hypertension in pregnancy that persists for 15 minutes should be treated with a first-line agent (IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or oral immediate-release nifedipine) as soon as possible, ideally within 30–60 minutes, to reduce the risk of maternal stroke.
Incorrect. Overly aggressive lowering can reduce uteroplacental perfusion; the usual target is about 140–150/90–100.
Incorrect. Supine positioning compresses the vena cava (supine hypotensive syndrome); a lateral position improves placental blood flow.
questions.rationale: Per ACOG guidance, persistent severe-range BP (systolic ≥160 or diastolic ≥110) in pregnancy is a hypertensive emergency. Timely treatment with IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or oral immediate-release nifedipine reduces the risk of maternal stroke. BP is lowered to a moderate range, not normal, to protect placental perfusion, and the client is positioned on her side.
questions.takeaway: Pregnancy BP ≥160/110 for 15 min → treat within 30–60 min; don't drop it to normal.
questions.hintContent: Recall the severe-range BP threshold in pregnancy and why maternal BP should not be lowered too far.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask how urgent this BP is for this population, then eliminate options that delay treatment or harm the fetus.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Peripheral Assessment · Carotid Arteries
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 70-year-old client with hypertension and hyperlipidemia reports that yesterday "a shade came down over my right eye" for about 5 minutes and then cleared. On auscultation, the nurse hears a low-pitched blowing sound over the right carotid artery. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: It is a sound transmitted from the aortic valve and does not require follow-up
It is a venous hum that will disappear if the client turns the head to the left
It should be confirmed by palpating both carotid arteries at the same time
It suggests turbulent flow from carotid stenosis and a high risk of stroke
optionRationales: Incorrect. A bruit with transient monocular vision loss must not be dismissed; transmitted murmurs are a diagnosis the provider makes after imaging.
Incorrect. A venous hum is continuous and heard over the jugular veins; this blowing sound over the artery with neurologic symptoms suggests arterial disease.
Incorrect. Carotids are never palpated simultaneously — this can reduce cerebral blood flow or trigger a vagal response.

Correct. A carotid bruit reflects turbulent flow, commonly from atherosclerotic stenosis. Transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax) on the same side is a TIA symptom, placing the client at high short-term stroke risk; the finding must be reported promptly.
questions.rationale: The bell of the stethoscope is used to auscultate carotid arteries for bruits. A bruit with ipsilateral transient monocular vision loss suggests carotid stenosis with a retinal TIA. The client needs urgent evaluation (carotid duplex ultrasound) because the risk of stroke is highest in the days after a TIA. Carotids are palpated one side at a time.
questions.takeaway: Carotid bruit + transient vision loss = TIA warning; report promptly and palpate one carotid at a time.
questions.hintContent: Recall what a bruit represents and the significance of transient monocular vision loss.
questions.hintStrategy: Connect the history (the symptom) with the physical finding; an option that dismisses a finding linked to symptoms is rarely correct.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Peripheral Assessment · Postoperative Vascular Checks
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client is 6 hours postoperative after a right femoral-popliteal bypass graft. Hourly Doppler checks of the right dorsalis pedis have shown a strong signal at the marked site. At 2200, the nurse cannot obtain a Doppler signal at the marked site or over the posterior tibial artery, the right foot is cool and pale, and the client reports new numbness of the toes. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Elevate the right leg on pillows and recheck the pulse in 1 hour
Wrap the right foot in a warm blanket and reassess in 30 minutes
Notify the surgeon immediately of the loss of the pulse signal
Document the findings and continue hourly neurovascular checks
optionRationales: Incorrect. Elevation reduces arterial inflow to an ischemic limb, and waiting an hour delays treatment of possible graft occlusion.
Incorrect. A light blanket for comfort is acceptable, but warmth does not restore flow, and delaying notification risks limb loss.
Correct. Loss of a previously present pulse with coolness, pallor, and new numbness suggests acute graft thrombosis — a surgical emergency requiring immediate notification.
Incorrect. Documentation alone fails to rescue the client; the change requires immediate action.
questions.rationale: After arterial bypass, the most important finding is a change from baseline. A pulse that was present and is now absent, with the 'Ps' of acute ischemia, signals graft occlusion. The nurse confirms quickly at the marked site (done here) and notifies the surgeon immediately, because revascularization delays lead to limb loss.
questions.takeaway: After bypass, a lost pulse is an emergency — call the surgeon now.
questions.hintContent: Recall why the pulse site is marked after vascular surgery and what a change from baseline means.
questions.hintStrategy: The stem asks what to do FIRST. The data already confirm the change, so choose the action that gets definitive help fastest.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Peripheral Assessment · Ankle-Brachial Index
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 68-year-old client with a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease reports calf pain when walking. The ankle-brachial index (ABI) is 1.52 on the right and 1.48 on the left. How should the nurse interpret these results?
options: The arteries are likely noncompressible; a toe-brachial index is needed
The results are normal, and PAD is excluded as the cause of the leg pain
The results indicate severe PAD with a high risk of limb loss
The results indicate the cuff was too large and the test should be repeated with a smaller cuff
optionRationales: Correct. An ABI >1.40 indicates noncompressible (calcified) arteries, common in long-standing diabetes and CKD. The result is falsely elevated and cannot exclude PAD; a toe-brachial index is used instead.
Incorrect. A normal ABI is 1.00–1.40; values above 1.40 are not 'extra normal' and can hide significant disease.
Incorrect. Severe PAD produces a LOW ABI (below 0.40), not a high one.
Incorrect. Cuff size problems do not explain bilaterally high values in a client with classic risk factors for medial calcification.
questions.rationale: ABI = ankle systolic pressure ÷ brachial systolic pressure. Normal is 1.00–1.40, 0.91–0.99 is borderline, ≤0.90 is abnormal, and >1.40 indicates noncompressible arteries. Diabetes and CKD cause medial arterial calcification, so the cuff cannot compress the vessel and the reading is falsely high. A toe-brachial index is recommended when ABI is >1.40.
questions.takeaway: ABI >1.40 = noncompressible arteries, not 'great circulation' — get a toe-brachial index.
questions.hintContent: Recall the ABI ranges and what calcification of the arterial wall does to cuff-based pressure measurement.
questions.hintStrategy: Notice that the value is ABOVE the normal range and link it to the risk factors in the stem.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Peripheral Assessment · Neurovascular Checks
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client is 10 hours postoperative after open reduction and internal fixation of a tibial fracture and has a posterior splint with an elastic wrap. The client rates pain 9/10 despite IV morphine 30 minutes ago. Pain increases sharply when the nurse passively extends the toes, and the calf feels tense. The pedal pulse is 2+ and capillary refill is 2 seconds. Which condition is the nurse's greatest concern?
options: Deep vein thrombosis of the calf
Acute compartment syndrome
Expected postoperative incisional pain
Acute arterial occlusion
optionRationales: Incorrect. DVT causes aching, swelling, and warmth, but not severe pain with passive stretch of the toes this soon after surgery.

Correct. Pain out of proportion to the injury, unrelieved by opioids and worsened by passive stretch, with a tense compartment, are early signs of compartment syndrome. Pulses often remain present until late.
Incorrect. Pain that escalates despite IV opioids and increases with passive stretch is not expected.
Incorrect. A 2+ pulse and brisk capillary refill show arterial inflow is intact.
questions.rationale: In compartment syndrome, pressure within a closed fascial compartment rises until it compromises capillary perfusion to muscle and nerve. Early signs are pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch; pulselessness is a LATE sign, so a palpable pulse does not rule it out. The nurse loosens the wrap, keeps the limb at heart level (not elevated), and notifies the provider immediately.
questions.takeaway: Pain out of proportion + pain on passive stretch = compartment syndrome, even with a pulse.
questions.hintContent: Recall the earliest versus the latest signs when pressure builds in a closed muscle compartment.
questions.hintStrategy: Do not let the normal pulse mislead you — ask which condition fits pain unrelieved by opioids and worsened by stretch.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Peripheral Assessment · Capillary Refill
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A client walks into the clinic from outside, where the temperature is 2 °C (35.6 °F). The client has no complaints. Vital signs are T 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), HR 76, BP 124/78. The nurse finds that capillary refill in the fingernails is 4 seconds and the fingers feel cold. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Document delayed capillary refill as evidence of hypovolemia
Notify the provider of impaired arterial perfusion to the hands
Obtain orthostatic vital signs to assess for fluid loss
Reassess capillary refill after the client's hands have warmed
optionRationales: Incorrect. Normal vital signs and no symptoms do not support hypovolemia; the finding is likely environmental.
Incorrect. Reporting is premature before ruling out a common, benign cause of the finding.
Incorrect. There are no cues suggesting fluid loss that would justify orthostatic testing.
Correct. Cold causes peripheral vasoconstriction, which prolongs capillary refill. Rewarming and reassessing provides an accurate result.
questions.rationale: Capillary refill is normally less than 2–3 seconds, but it is prolonged by cold, vasoconstriction, and poor lighting as well as by hypovolemia or arterial disease. The nurse interprets a finding in context: with stable vital signs and recent cold exposure, the best action is to warm the hands and reassess before drawing conclusions.
questions.takeaway: Cold hands lengthen capillary refill — warm and recheck before you label it abnormal.
questions.hintContent: Recall the factors other than circulatory disease that can prolong capillary refill.
questions.hintStrategy: Look at the whole context (environment, vital signs, symptoms) before assuming a single finding indicates pathology.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Shock (Hypovolemic)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with an upper gastrointestinal bleed has vomited 600 mL of bright red blood. HR is 128, BP 82/50, and the client is pale and diaphoretic. The only IV access is a 22-gauge catheter in the hand. The provider prescribes 1 L of lactated Ringer's solution and 2 units of packed red blood cells. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Insert two large-bore (16- or 18-gauge) peripheral IV catheters
Infuse the lactated Ringer's through the 22-gauge catheter using a rapid infuser
Place the client in a steep head-down Trendelenburg position
Wait for the type and crossmatch before starting any fluid
optionRationales: Correct. Flow rate depends on catheter radius; large-bore access allows rapid volume and blood replacement in hemorrhagic shock.
Incorrect. A 22-gauge catheter limits flow and is not recommended for rapid transfusion of blood products.
Incorrect. Steep Trendelenburg is no longer recommended; it impairs ventilation and gives little sustained BP benefit. Keeping the client flat or raising the legs is preferred.
Incorrect. Crystalloid resuscitation should begin immediately while blood products are prepared.
questions.rationale: In hypovolemic (hemorrhagic) shock, the priority is restoring circulating volume. Large-bore IV access (two 16- to 18-gauge catheters) permits rapid infusion of warmed isotonic crystalloid and blood. Positioning with legs elevated, oxygen, and monitoring of HR, BP, urine output, and mental status follow.
questions.takeaway: Hemorrhagic shock: two large-bore IVs, fluids and blood, flat with legs up — not steep Trendelenburg.
questions.hintContent: Recall how catheter size affects flow rate and what access is needed to transfuse blood rapidly.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask which option removes the biggest barrier to carrying out the provider's resuscitation orders.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 74-year-old client with a 5.8-cm abdominal aortic aneurysm is awaiting elective repair. The client suddenly reports severe, constant back and flank pain. HR is 124, BP 86/52, and the skin is pale and cool. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Palpate the abdomen to compare the size of the pulsatile mass with the earlier assessment
Administer the prescribed PRN oral oxycodone and reassess the pain in 30 minutes
Activate the rapid response team and notify the surgeon of suspected rupture
Obtain a 12-lead ECG to evaluate for an acute myocardial infarction
optionRationales: Incorrect. Deep palpation of a known aneurysm is avoided and delays emergency care.
Incorrect. Treating pain without addressing hypotension and tachycardia misses a life-threatening hemorrhage.
Correct. Sudden severe back or flank pain with shock in a client with a large AAA indicates rupture, which requires immediate surgical intervention.
Incorrect. An ECG may be obtained, but the findings point to aortic rupture, and definitive help is needed first.
questions.rationale: A ruptured AAA causes sudden severe abdominal, back, or flank pain with signs of hemorrhagic shock. Mortality is extremely high, and survival depends on immediate surgical repair. The nurse summons help at once, then establishes large-bore IV access and prepares the client for surgery.
questions.takeaway: Known AAA + sudden back pain + hypotension = rupture — get the team and surgeon now.
questions.hintContent: Recall the classic presentation of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the life-threatening condition first; then pick the action that addresses it rather than a symptom or an alternate diagnosis.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Shock · Vasopressors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client in septic shock is receiving a norepinephrine infusion through an 18-gauge peripheral IV in the right forearm while central line placement is being arranged. The nurse notes blanching, coolness, and swelling of the skin around the insertion site. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Apply a cold compress and elevate the arm
Slow the infusion rate by half and reassess the site in 15 minutes
Remove the catheter immediately and apply firm pressure to the site
Stop the norepinephrine infusion at that site
optionRationales: Incorrect. Cold causes further vasoconstriction and worsens tissue ischemia from a vasopressor extravasation.
Incorrect. Any continued infusion into the tissue increases the risk of necrosis.
Incorrect. Guidelines typically advise leaving the catheter briefly to attempt aspiration of the drug before removal; immediate removal is not the first step.

Correct. Stopping the infusion at the extravasated site limits tissue injury. The nurse then notifies the provider, prepares phentolamine for local infiltration as prescribed, and restarts the vasopressor through another line promptly.
questions.rationale: Norepinephrine is a vesicant; extravasation causes intense local vasoconstriction and can lead to tissue necrosis. The first action is to stop the infusion into the affected site. Phentolamine, an alpha-adrenergic blocker, is infiltrated around the site per protocol. Because the client depends on the vasopressor, new access must be obtained quickly to prevent hypotension.
questions.takeaway: Vasopressor extravasation: stop the infusion at that site, phentolamine, new access fast — no cold packs.
questions.hintContent: Recall how an alpha-adrenergic vasopressor affects local tissue and which drug is its antidote.
questions.hintStrategy: The stem asks what to do FIRST. Choose the action that stops ongoing harm before the actions that treat it.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Prioritization
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: After receiving hand-off report on a medical unit, which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with PAD who reports calf cramping after walking to the bathroom that resolved after resting 3 minutes
A client with heart failure who gained 1.5 kg (3.3 lb) overnight and has new bibasilar crackles
A client 2 days after an ischemic stroke, not treated with a thrombolytic, whose BP is 176/98
A client with a venous stasis ulcer whose dressing is saturated with serous drainage
optionRationales: Not first. Claudication that resolves with rest is expected, chronic, and stable.
First. A 1.5-kg overnight gain with new crackles indicates acute fluid retention and worsening pulmonary congestion that threatens breathing.
Not first. Permissive hypertension (treated only if ≥220/120) is expected after an ischemic stroke when no thrombolytic was given.
Not first. Venous ulcers drain heavily; the dressing needs changing but it is not an airway, breathing, or circulation threat.
questions.rationale: Prioritize using ABCs and unstable over stable. The client with heart failure has rapid fluid gain with new pulmonary congestion — an acute threat to breathing. Stable claudication, expected permissive hypertension after stroke, and ulcer drainage are chronic or expected findings.
questions.takeaway: Rapid weight gain + new crackles in HF = see first.
questions.hintContent: Recall what is expected in stable PAD, after an ischemic stroke without thrombolysis, and with venous ulcers.
questions.hintStrategy: Classify each client as expected/stable or new/unstable, then apply ABCs to the unstable one(s).

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Case Study B.E. · Stroke Rehabilitation
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: B.E., 64, is recovering from an ischemic stroke of the right parietal-temporal region. He has left-sided weakness, leaves the food on the left side of his tray untouched, and has bumped his left arm on the doorframe twice. Which intervention is most appropriate to include in his plan of care?
options: Teach B.E. to turn his head and scan to the left side of his environment
Place the call light and water pitcher on his left side so he is forced to use that side
Use picture boards because he cannot understand spoken language
Keep him on bed rest until the inattention to his left side resolves
optionRationales: Correct. Unilateral neglect after a right-hemisphere stroke is managed by teaching visual scanning toward the neglected side, which improves safety and function.
Incorrect. Essential items should be on the side he attends to (the right) until he learns to compensate; placing them on the neglected side creates a safety risk.
Incorrect. Receptive aphasia is typical of left-hemisphere (dominant) stroke; B.E.'s right-hemisphere stroke causes neglect and impulsivity instead.
Incorrect. Prolonged bed rest increases the risk of complications and does not treat neglect; early mobilization with supervision is preferred.
questions.rationale: Right-hemisphere strokes commonly cause left-sided weakness, unilateral neglect, impaired judgment, and impulsivity. Teaching the client to scan toward the neglected side, protecting the affected arm, and keeping essential items within the attended field promote safety and rehabilitation.
questions.takeaway: Right-brain stroke → left neglect: teach scanning left, keep essentials within reach on the attended side.
questions.hintContent: Recall the typical deficits of a right-hemisphere versus a left-hemisphere stroke.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the deficit from the behavior described, then select the intervention that treats that specific deficit safely.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Peripheral Artery Disease · Teaching
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse taught a client with peripheral artery disease and intermittent claudication about self-care. Which statement by the client indicates the teaching was effective?
options: "I'll raise my legs on pillows above my heart when they ache at night."
"I'll walk until the cramping starts, rest until it stops, then walk again."
"A heating pad on my feet at bedtime will help open up my narrowed blood vessels."
"Cutting down to five cigarettes a day will protect my circulation."
optionRationales: Needs further teaching. Elevation reduces arterial flow; legs should be level or slightly dependent in arterial disease.
Effective. Structured walking to near-maximal claudication, resting, and resuming (30–45 minutes, at least 3 times per week) builds collateral circulation and increases walking distance.
Needs further teaching. Reduced sensation and poor blood flow increase the risk of burns from heating pads.
Needs further teaching. Any amount of smoking causes vasoconstriction and progression of atherosclerosis; complete cessation is the goal.
questions.rationale: Exercise therapy (ideally supervised) is a first-line treatment for claudication, improving walking distance through collateral development and muscle adaptation. Complete smoking cessation, foot protection, and avoiding leg elevation and direct heat are key teaching points for arterial disease.
questions.takeaway: PAD: walk–rest–walk, stop smoking completely, legs down, no heating pads.
questions.hintContent: Recall how exercise, positioning, heat, and smoking affect arterial blood flow.
questions.hintStrategy: This item asks for the CORRECT statement. Test each statement against the principle 'improve arterial inflow and protect tissue.'

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Heart Failure · Pharmacology
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction took lisinopril 10 mg at 0800 today. The provider discontinues lisinopril and prescribes sacubitril/valsartan 24/26 mg PO twice daily, with the first dose due at 2000 tonight. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Administer the first dose at 2000 as prescribed
Administer the first dose with an antihistamine to prevent a reaction
Contact the prescriber about the timing of the first dose
Give both lisinopril and sacubitril/valsartan tomorrow for added benefit
optionRationales: Incorrect. Giving the dose only 12 hours after an ACE inhibitor increases the risk of angioedema.
Incorrect. Antihistamine premedication does not prevent bradykinin-mediated angioedema and is not the standard of care.
Correct. Sacubitril/valsartan is contraindicated within 36 hours of the last ACE inhibitor dose because combined inhibition of bradykinin breakdown increases the risk of angioedema.
Incorrect. Concurrent use of an ACE inhibitor and sacubitril/valsartan is contraindicated.
questions.rationale: Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin, and ACE inhibitors block bradykinin breakdown; combining them (or overlapping within 36 hours) greatly increases the risk of angioedema. The nurse verifies the timing with the prescriber before giving the first dose.
questions.takeaway: ACE inhibitor → ARNI switch needs a 36-hour washout.
questions.hintContent: Recall the mechanism shared by ACE inhibitors and neprilysin inhibitors that raises the risk of angioedema.
questions.hintStrategy: Check the TIMES in the stem; the medication itself is appropriate, so ask whether it is safe to give it now.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Delegation
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse is working with an unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) on a cardiac unit. Which task is appropriate for the nurse to delegate to the UAP?
options: Checking the color and warmth of the toes of a client who reports new numbness in one foot
Evaluating whether a client's leg pain improved after a PRN analgesic
Teaching a client with hypertension how to use a home blood pressure monitor
Measuring the daily weight of a stable client with heart failure
optionRationales: Incorrect. A new symptom requires RN assessment and clinical judgment.
Incorrect. Evaluating the effect of a medication is an RN responsibility.
Incorrect. Initial teaching is within RN scope and cannot be delegated to a UAP.
Correct. Measuring weight and recording I&O on a stable client are routine, standardized tasks with predictable outcomes; the nurse interprets the data.
questions.rationale: UAPs can perform routine, standardized tasks for stable clients, such as weights, vital signs, and I&O. Assessment of new symptoms, evaluation of interventions, and teaching require RN clinical judgment and cannot be delegated. The RN remains accountable for interpreting data the UAP collects.
questions.takeaway: Delegate collecting data on stable clients; keep assessing, teaching, and evaluating.
questions.hintContent: Recall the five rights of delegation and which activities require RN judgment.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the words 'new,' 'evaluate,' and 'teach' — they signal tasks that stay with the RN.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Collaborative Therapies · Statins
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client started on atorvastatin 40 mg daily 3 weeks ago tells the nurse, "My thighs ache and feel weak. I figured it was from gardening." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: "Muscle aches can be a side effect. I'll let your provider know."
"This is expected when you start a statin and will go away in a few months."
"Take your atorvastatin with a glass of grapefruit juice to reduce the aches."
"Stop all of your heart medicines until the aching goes away."
optionRationales: Correct. Unexplained muscle pain or weakness can signal statin-associated myopathy (rarely rhabdomyolysis); the provider may check a CK level and adjust therapy.
Incorrect. Muscle symptoms should not be dismissed as expected; they need evaluation.
Incorrect. Grapefruit juice raises atorvastatin levels and INCREASES the risk of myopathy.
Incorrect. The client should not stop all cardiac medications; this could be dangerous. Changes are directed by the provider.
questions.rationale: Statins lower LDL cholesterol but can cause myopathy. Clients are taught to report unexplained muscle pain, weakness, or dark urine. Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4 metabolism of some statins (including atorvastatin), increasing drug levels and myopathy risk.
questions.takeaway: Statin + unexplained muscle pain = report (check CK); avoid large amounts of grapefruit juice.
questions.hintContent: Recall the most important musculoskeletal adverse effect of statins and what increases its risk.
questions.hintStrategy: Avoid responses that dismiss a symptom or advise the client to change medications without the provider.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Chest Pain · Nitroglycerin Safety
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client arrives at the emergency department with substernal chest pressure rated 7/10. BP is 138/84, HR 92. The provider prescribes nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingually every 5 minutes for up to 3 doses. During the medication history, the client states he took sildenafil 12 hours ago. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Give the nitroglycerin and check BP 5 minutes after each dose
Give one nitroglycerin tablet instead of three and monitor closely
Withhold the nitroglycerin and notify the provider of the sildenafil use
Give the nitroglycerin because more than 6 hours have passed since the sildenafil
optionRationales: Incorrect. Monitoring does not prevent the severe, refractory hypotension that can result from this combination.
Incorrect. Even a single dose is contraindicated within the interaction window.
Correct. Nitrates are contraindicated within 24 hours of sildenafil (48 hours for tadalafil) because both increase nitric oxide–mediated vasodilation, causing profound hypotension.
Incorrect. The contraindication window for sildenafil is 24 hours, not 6 hours.
questions.rationale: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors potentiate the vasodilating effect of nitrates, which can cause life-threatening hypotension and reduced coronary perfusion. Nitrates are avoided within 24 hours of sildenafil or vardenafil and 48 hours of tadalafil. Nurses must ask about these drugs before giving nitrates.
questions.takeaway: Ask about PDE-5 inhibitors before nitrates: 24 h for sildenafil, 48 h for tadalafil.
questions.hintContent: Recall the interaction between nitrates and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and the time windows involved.
questions.hintStrategy: Focus on the new piece of information in the medication history — it changes whether the prescription is safe.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Hypertension · Lifestyle Modification
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse is planning teaching for a 52-year-old client newly diagnosed with stage 2 hypertension who has a BMI of 31 and normal kidney function. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Follow a DASH-style eating plan rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy
Aim for less than 2,300 mg of sodium per day, working toward about 1,500 mg
Get at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity each week
Limit alcohol to no more than 3 drinks per day
Stop the BP medication once home readings are consistently below 130/80
Losing weight lowers BP; each kilogram lost lowers systolic BP about 1 mm Hg
optionRationales: Correct. The DASH diet can lower systolic BP by roughly 8–11 mm Hg in people with hypertension.
Correct. Sodium reduction is recommended; an optimal goal is about 1,500 mg/day, and any reduction helps.
Correct. Regular aerobic activity (about 150 min/week) lowers BP by roughly 5–8 mm Hg.
Incorrect. Recommended limits are no more than 2 drinks/day for men and 1 for women (or less); 3 drinks/day raises BP.
Incorrect. Controlled readings show the medication is working; stopping it causes BP to rise again. Changes are made only with the provider.
Correct. Weight loss is one of the most effective lifestyle measures — about 1 mm Hg per kg lost.
questions.rationale: Evidence-based lifestyle measures for hypertension include weight loss, a DASH-style diet, sodium reduction, increased potassium intake (if kidney function is normal), regular physical activity, and moderation of alcohol. These are added to, not substituted for, prescribed medication in stage 2 hypertension.
questions.takeaway: Lifestyle for HTN: lose weight, DASH, less sodium, move 150 min/wk, limit alcohol — and keep taking the pills.
questions.hintContent: Recall the AHA/ACC nonpharmacologic interventions for hypertension and the recommended alcohol limits.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option independently as true or false. Watch for options with an incorrect number or a dangerous misconception.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Hypertensive Emergency
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: 1100 (ICU admission): 56-year-old client with untreated hypertension. Severe headache, new confusion, and blurred vision. Retinal hemorrhages noted by provider. BP 224/132 (right arm) confirmed on repeat; HR 98; RR 20; SpO₂ 96% RA. Creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.0). No chest pain; no signs of aortic dissection.

tabs.title: Orders
tabs.html:
• Nicardipine IV infusion; titrate per protocol
  • Radial arterial line
  • Neurologic checks per ICU protocol
  • Strict intake and output

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes and Orders. Which actions should the nurse take while caring for this client? Select all that apply.
options: Monitor BP continuously via the arterial line during titration
Titrate to reduce the systolic BP by no more than 25% within the first hour
Titrate the infusion to reach a BP of 120/80 within the first 30 minutes
Perform frequent neurologic assessments for changes in mental status
Measure hourly urine output
Infuse the nicardipine by gravity so the rate can be adjusted quickly
optionRationales: Correct. Continuous intra-arterial monitoring allows precise, safe titration of a potent vasodilator.
Correct. Without a compelling condition, SBP is lowered by no more than 25% in the first hour, then to 160/100 over the next 2–6 hours, then cautiously toward normal over 24–48 hours.
Incorrect. Rapid normalization can cause cerebral, coronary, or renal ischemia because autoregulation has shifted to higher pressures.
Correct. Hypertensive encephalopathy is present; worsening or improving neurologic status guides therapy and detects hypoperfusion from overcorrection.
Correct. Acute kidney injury is present; urine output tracks renal perfusion during treatment.
Incorrect. Titrated vasoactive infusions must run on an infusion pump for precise dosing.
questions.rationale: A hypertensive emergency (BP >180/120 with acute target-organ damage — here encephalopathy, retinal hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury) requires ICU care with a titratable IV agent. BP is lowered in a controlled manner (≤25% in the first hour) while target organs are monitored, because chronically hypertensive vascular beds become ischemic if pressure falls too fast.
questions.takeaway: Hypertensive emergency: IV titratable drug on a pump, arterial line, ≤25% drop in hour 1, watch brain and kidneys.
questions.hintContent: Recall why cerebral autoregulation makes rapid BP reduction dangerous and which organs are being damaged in this client.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option on its own. Eliminate options that lower BP too fast or that compromise medication safety.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Peripheral Assessment · Venous Thromboembolism
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client 3 days after a left total knee arthroplasty. Which findings should the nurse recognize as possible signs of deep vein thrombosis (DVT)? Select all that apply.
options: Left calf circumference 3 cm larger than the right
Warmth and redness over the left calf
Aching tenderness in the left calf when standing
Bilateral ankle edema that resolves overnight
Pale, cool left foot with a diminished pedal pulse
Calf pain on dorsiflexion, which confirms the diagnosis
optionRationales: Correct. Unilateral swelling of the affected leg (commonly >2–3 cm difference) is a key sign of venous obstruction.
Correct. Warmth and erythema over the vein reflect inflammation and venous congestion.
Correct. Aching, tenderness, or heaviness of the calf, often worse with standing or walking, is common.
Incorrect. Bilateral dependent edema that resolves with elevation suggests a systemic or chronic venous process, not an acute DVT.
Incorrect. A pale, cool limb with a weak pulse indicates arterial insufficiency; DVT typically causes a warm, swollen limb.
Incorrect. Homans' sign is unreliable and nonspecific; it does not confirm or rule out DVT. Diagnosis requires duplex ultrasound.
questions.rationale: Many DVTs are asymptomatic, but classic signs include unilateral leg swelling, warmth, erythema, and calf tenderness. Findings should be reported, and duplex venous ultrasound confirms the diagnosis. Arterial findings (pallor, coolness, diminished pulses) point to a different problem, and Homans' sign is not a reliable test.
questions.takeaway: DVT: one leg, warm, swollen, tender — confirm with ultrasound, not Homans' sign.
questions.hintContent: Recall how venous obstruction changes the appearance of a limb compared with arterial obstruction.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask for each option: is it unilateral, and does it fit a venous (warm, swollen) rather than arterial (pale, cool) picture?

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Lifespan: Older Adult with PAD and Diabetes
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse is teaching foot care to a 78-year-old client with type 2 diabetes and peripheral artery disease who has impaired vision and lives with an adult daughter. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Have your daughter inspect your feet daily for cuts, blisters, or color changes
Wear well-fitting shoes and socks and never walk barefoot
Soak your feet in hot water each evening to improve circulation
Warm cold feet with a heating pad at bedtime
Have a podiatrist trim your toenails
Apply moisturizing lotion between your toes after bathing
optionRationales: Correct. Daily inspection catches injuries early; with impaired vision, a family member or a mirror is needed.
Correct. Protective footwear prevents unnoticed injuries in a client with reduced sensation and poor healing.
Incorrect. Hot soaks risk burns (reduced sensation) and macerate the skin; lukewarm water tested with the elbow or a thermometer is safe.
Incorrect. Direct heat on ischemic, insensate tissue can cause burns.
Correct. With poor vision and PAD, professional nail care reduces the risk of cuts and infection.
Incorrect. Lotion is applied to dry skin on the tops and soles, but not between the toes, where moisture promotes fungal infection and maceration.
questions.rationale: Older adults with diabetes and PAD have reduced sensation, poor perfusion, and slow healing, so minor foot injuries can lead to ulcers and amputation. Teaching is adapted to the client's age-related vision loss by involving the family and a podiatrist, and emphasizes daily inspection, protective footwear, and avoidance of heat and moisture between the toes.
questions.takeaway: Diabetic/PAD feet: look daily (with help), shoes always, no heat, dry between toes, podiatrist for nails.
questions.hintContent: Recall how reduced sensation and reduced blood flow change the risks of heat, moisture, and minor injury to the feet.
questions.hintStrategy: Consider the client's age and vision in the stem — the correct options should be safe for someone who cannot see or feel foot injuries well.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Acute Ischemic Stroke · Thrombolytic Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with an acute ischemic stroke received IV tenecteplase 45 minutes ago and has been admitted to the stroke unit. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Perform neurologic checks and vital signs every 15 minutes as prescribed
Maintain BP below 180/105 mm Hg
Avoid inserting a nasogastric tube or indwelling urinary catheter unless essential
Administer aspirin 325 mg now to prevent re-occlusion
Report a sudden severe headache or worsening neurologic status immediately
Encourage oral fluids now that the clot has been dissolved
optionRationales: Correct. Standard post-thrombolysis monitoring is every 15 minutes for 2 hours, every 30 minutes for 6 hours, then hourly until 24 hours.
Correct. BP is kept below 180/105 for 24 hours after thrombolysis to reduce the risk of intracranial hemorrhage.
Correct. Invasive procedures are delayed when possible because of the bleeding risk after a thrombolytic.
Incorrect. Antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs are generally withheld for 24 hours after thrombolysis, until a follow-up scan excludes hemorrhage.
Correct. Headache, nausea/vomiting, acute hypertension, or neurologic decline may signal intracranial hemorrhage and require an emergency CT.
Incorrect. The client remains NPO until a bedside swallow screen is passed, regardless of reperfusion.
questions.rationale: After IV thrombolysis (tenecteplase or alteplase), nursing care focuses on detecting hemorrhage and neurologic change: frequent neurologic checks and vital signs, BP <180/105, avoiding invasive procedures, withholding antithrombotics for 24 hours, and keeping the client NPO until the swallow screen is passed.
questions.takeaway: Post-thrombolysis: q15 min neuro/VS, BP <180/105, no antithrombotics or invasive lines for 24 h, NPO until swallow screen.
questions.hintContent: Recall the main complication of thrombolytic therapy and the BP target after treatment.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask whether it would increase or help detect bleeding, and whether it respects the swallow-screen rule.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Heart Failure · Medication Monitoring
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with heart failure takes lisinopril 20 mg daily and spironolactone 25 mg daily. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.
options: Serum potassium of 5.8 mEq/L
Swelling of the lips and tongue
BP of 84/50 with dizziness on standing
BP of 118/72 with no symptoms
Serum sodium of 138 mEq/L
Urine output of 1,800 mL in 24 hours
optionRationales: Report. Both drugs cause potassium retention; hyperkalemia can cause life-threatening dysrhythmias.
Report immediately. Angioedema is a potentially fatal adverse effect of ACE inhibitors that can obstruct the airway.
Report. Symptomatic hypotension is an adverse effect of ACE inhibitors, especially with volume depletion.
Do not report as a problem. This is a desirable BP for a client with heart failure.
Do not report as a problem. This sodium level is within normal limits.
Do not report as a problem. This is an adequate urine output.
questions.rationale: ACE inhibitors and aldosterone antagonists improve survival in HFrEF but share the risk of hyperkalemia; ACE inhibitors also cause hypotension, cough, and angioedema. Nurses monitor potassium, renal function, and BP and report abnormal values or signs of angioedema promptly.
questions.takeaway: ACE inhibitor + spironolactone: watch K⁺, BP, and angioedema.
questions.hintContent: Recall the effect of ACE inhibitors and aldosterone antagonists on potassium and their other major adverse effects.
questions.hintStrategy: Treat each option as a separate true/false decision: is this value abnormal or dangerous for this drug combination?

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Independent Interventions · Venous Return
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client is on postoperative day 1 after abdominal surgery and spends most of the day in bed. Which independent nursing interventions promote venous return and help prevent venous stasis? Select all that apply.
options: Encourage ankle pumps and leg exercises every hour while awake
Avoid placing pillows under the knees
Encourage the client to cross the legs at the knees for comfort
Assist with early ambulation as soon as allowed
Massage the calves firmly twice daily
Limit oral fluids to reduce the risk of edema
optionRationales: Correct. Contracting the calf muscles pumps blood toward the heart.
Correct. Pillows under the knees compress the popliteal vein and impede venous flow.
Incorrect. Crossing the legs compresses veins and promotes stasis.
Correct. Walking is one of the most effective ways to activate the calf-muscle pump.
Incorrect. Massage is avoided because it could dislodge an undetected thrombus.
Incorrect. Dehydration increases blood viscosity and clot risk; adequate hydration is encouraged unless restricted.
questions.rationale: Virchow's triad (stasis, vessel injury, hypercoagulability) explains postoperative VTE risk. Independent nursing measures that reduce stasis include leg exercises, early ambulation, avoiding knee pillows and leg crossing, and adequate hydration. Massaging the legs is avoided.
questions.takeaway: Move the calves, walk early, hydrate — no knee pillows, crossed legs, or leg massage.
questions.hintContent: Recall how the calf-muscle pump works and what compresses or slows venous flow in the legs.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask of each option: does it speed venous blood back to the heart, or does it compress veins or thicken the blood?

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Heart Failure · Discharge Teaching
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse is preparing discharge teaching for a client with heart failure. Which changes should the nurse instruct the client to report to the provider? Select all that apply.
options: Weight gain of 1 kg (2–3 lb) in a day or 2 kg (5 lb) in a week
Needing more pillows than usual to sleep
New or increasing swelling in the ankles or feet
Urinating more often in the hours after taking furosemide
Mild tiredness after grocery shopping that goes away with rest
Feeling thirsty while following the fluid limit
optionRationales: Correct. Rapid weight gain reflects fluid retention and often precedes worsening symptoms.
Correct. Increasing orthopnea signals worsening pulmonary congestion.
Correct. New or worsening edema indicates fluid retention and systemic venous congestion.
Incorrect. Increased urination is the expected effect of a diuretic.
Incorrect. Mild fatigue that resolves with rest is expected with HF; new or worsening exercise intolerance would be reported.
Incorrect. Thirst is common with fluid restriction; ice chips or sugar-free hard candy can help.
questions.rationale: Clients with heart failure are taught to weigh daily and to recognize early signs of decompensation — rapid weight gain, increased orthopnea or dyspnea, and worsening edema — so treatment can be adjusted before hospitalization is needed. Expected medication effects and mild, stable fatigue do not require a call.
questions.takeaway: HF red flags at home: fast weight gain, more pillows, more swelling.
questions.hintContent: Recall the early signs of fluid retention and pulmonary congestion in heart failure.
questions.hintStrategy: Separate expected effects of treatment or of the chronic condition from NEW changes that suggest worsening.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure · Palpatory–Auscultatory Technique
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is measuring blood pressure manually for a 76-year-old client with long-standing hypertension, using a palpated estimate to avoid missing an auscultatory gap. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Have the client sit quietly for 5 minutes with back supported, feet flat, and arm supported at heart level
Wrap a correctly sized cuff on the bare upper arm with the bladder centered over the brachial artery
Palpate the radial pulse and inflate the cuff until the pulse disappears, noting that pressure
Deflate the cuff completely and wait at least 30 seconds
Inflate to 30 mm Hg above the palpated pressure and deflate at 2–3 mm Hg per second, noting phases I and V
questions.rationale: Rest and correct positioning come first so the reading reflects baseline BP. The cuff is applied to bare skin. The palpated systolic estimate tells the nurse how high to inflate, preventing a falsely low systolic reading if an auscultatory gap is present (common in older adults with arterial stiffness). The cuff is fully deflated and allowed to rest before inflating to 30 mm Hg above the estimate and deflating slowly; the first sound (phase I) is systolic and the disappearance of sounds (phase V) is diastolic in adults.
questions.takeaway: Rest → cuff on bare arm → palpate estimate → deflate/wait → inflate 30 above, deflate 2–3 mm Hg/s.
questions.hintContent: Recall why a palpated systolic estimate is obtained and how an auscultatory gap causes errors.
questions.hintStrategy: Think about what must be in place before any measurement, then which measurement informs the next one.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Peripheral Assessment · Ankle-Brachial Index
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is obtaining an ankle-brachial index (ABI) with a handheld Doppler for a client with suspected peripheral artery disease. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Position the client supine and allow at least 5–10 minutes of rest
Measure the systolic pressure in both arms using the brachial artery Doppler signal
Measure the systolic pressure at the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries of each ankle
Divide the higher ankle pressure for each leg by the higher of the two brachial pressures
Compare each result with reference ranges and report a value of 0.90 or less
questions.rationale: The client rests supine so that arm and ankle pressures are measured at the same hydrostatic level. Brachial pressures are obtained in both arms (the higher is the denominator). Ankle pressures are measured at both pedal arteries on each side, and the higher value for each leg is the numerator. An ABI of 0.90 or less indicates PAD; values above 1.40 indicate noncompressible arteries.
questions.takeaway: ABI = higher ankle pressure (each leg) ÷ higher brachial pressure; ≤0.90 = PAD.
questions.hintContent: Recall the ABI formula and why the client must rest supine first.
questions.hintStrategy: Preparation comes first, data collection next, then calculation, and interpretation last.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Peripheral Assessment · Doppler Pulse
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse cannot palpate the dorsalis pedis pulse of a client with peripheral artery disease and will use a handheld Doppler. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Explain the procedure and expose the top of the foot
Apply ultrasound gel over the expected location of the pulse
Place the probe at a 45° angle and move it slowly until a pulsatile signal is heard
Mark the location of the pulse on the skin with an indelible pen
Wipe the gel from the skin and probe, and document the findings
questions.rationale: After explaining the procedure, gel is applied to conduct the ultrasound waves. The probe is held at about a 45° angle and moved slowly until the arterial signal is heard. Marking the site lets every nurse reassess in the same place, which is essential for detecting changes. The gel is then removed, and findings (e.g., 'Doppler signal present') are documented.
questions.takeaway: Doppler: explain → gel → probe at 45° → mark the spot → clean and document.
questions.hintContent: Recall why a marked pulse site improves the reliability of serial assessments.
questions.hintStrategy: Follow the natural flow: prepare the client, conduct the signal, find it, preserve the location, then finish.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure · Orthostatic Hypotension
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse reviews orthostatic vital signs (supine after 5 minutes of rest → standing at 3 minutes) for several clients. For each client, indicate whether the findings meet the criteria for orthostatic hypotension.
optionRationales: Meets criteria. Systolic drop of 24 mm Hg (≥20).
Does not meet criteria. Systolic drop of 6 and diastolic drop of 4 are within normal postural change.
Meets criteria. Although the systolic drop is only 8, the diastolic drop is 12 mm Hg (≥10).
Does not meet criteria. The BP is low-normal, but the drop (4/2) is small; a low baseline alone is not orthostatic hypotension.
Meets criteria. Systolic drop of 22 mm Hg; the minimal HR rise may suggest a neurogenic cause or beta-blocker effect.
questions.rationale: Orthostatic hypotension is a sustained drop in systolic BP of at least 20 mm Hg or diastolic BP of at least 10 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing. Either criterion alone is sufficient. The nurse evaluates the change, not the absolute value, and uses the result to plan fall prevention and report to the provider.
questions.takeaway: Orthostatic: SBP ↓ ≥20 OR DBP ↓ ≥10 within 3 minutes of standing.
questions.hintContent: Recall the systolic and diastolic thresholds used to define orthostatic hypotension.
questions.hintStrategy: Calculate both the systolic and diastolic change for every row — one criterion is enough.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Venous Insufficiency · Nursing Care
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client with chronic venous insufficiency has a shallow, moist ulcer above the medial malleolus, brownish skin discoloration, and 2+ ankle edema. The ankle-brachial index is 1.05. For each intervention, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated.
rows: Elevate the legs above heart level several times a day
Keep the legs dependent to increase blood flow to the ulcer
Sit for long periods with the legs crossed
Walk daily to activate the calf-muscle pump
optionRationales: Indicated. Elevation uses gravity to reduce venous pressure and edema, promoting healing.
Indicated. Compression is the cornerstone of venous ulcer treatment; a normal ABI confirms adequate arterial flow so compression is safe.
Contraindicated. Dependency increases venous pressure and edema; it is used for arterial, not venous, disease.
Contraindicated. Prolonged sitting and leg crossing increase venous stasis.
Indicated. Walking contracts the calf muscles, pushing venous blood toward the heart.
questions.rationale: Venous ulcers result from venous hypertension. Care focuses on reducing venous pressure: elevation, compression (after arterial disease is excluded, e.g., ABI ≥0.8–0.9), walking, and avoiding prolonged standing, sitting, and leg crossing. Dependency helps arterial perfusion but worsens venous disease.
questions.takeaway: Venous: elevate, compress, walk. Arterial: dependent, no compression.
questions.hintContent: Recall how venous hypertension causes ulcers and why the ABI matters before compression.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the type of vascular problem first, then decide whether each intervention lowers or raises venous pressure.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Hypertension · Medication Teaching
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: The nurse has taught a client who takes hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril, and clonidine for resistant hypertension. For each client statement, indicate whether it shows understanding or a need for further teaching.
rows: "I'll sit on the side of the bed for a minute before I stand up."
"If my blood pressure is normal for a week, I can skip my pills."
"I'll keep a log of my home blood pressure readings and bring it to each visit."
"If the clonidine makes me sleepy, I'll stop it on my own."
"I'll call my provider right away if my lips or tongue start to swell."
optionRationales: Shows understanding. Changing position slowly reduces the risk of orthostatic hypotension and falls.
Needs further teaching. Normal readings reflect medication effect; skipping doses causes BP to rise again.
Shows understanding. Home monitoring logs guide medication adjustment.
Needs further teaching. Abruptly stopping clonidine can cause severe rebound hypertension; it must be tapered by the provider.
Shows understanding. Angioedema from an ACE inhibitor is an emergency that can obstruct the airway.
questions.rationale: Adherence is the biggest barrier to BP control. Clients learn to rise slowly, monitor BP at home, never stop medications abruptly (especially clonidine, which causes rebound hypertension), and recognize serious adverse effects such as ACE-inhibitor angioedema.
questions.takeaway: Never stop clonidine abruptly; never skip pills because BP is 'normal.'
questions.hintContent: Recall the dangers of abruptly stopping clonidine and the serious adverse effect of ACE inhibitors.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each statement independently; statements that involve the client changing medications on their own are red flags.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Shock · Types of Shock
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing findings for clients in shock. For each finding, indicate the type of shock it most likely represents.
rows: Warm, flushed skin and T 39.2 °C (102.6 °F) in a client with pneumonia
Jugular venous distention, crackles, and cool, clammy skin after an anterior MI
Flat neck veins, thirst, and cool, pale skin after 1,500 mL of blood loss
Lactate 4.8 mmol/L and WBC 22,000/mm³ with a known urinary tract infection
New S3 and BNP 1,900 pg/mL with falling BP and urine output
optionRationales: Septic. Early septic (distributive) shock causes vasodilation with warm, flushed skin and fever from infection.
Cardiogenic. Pump failure backs blood into the lungs (crackles) and veins (JVD) while low output causes vasoconstriction.
Hypovolemic. Loss of volume leaves the neck veins flat and triggers thirst and vasoconstriction.
Septic. Infection with leukocytosis and elevated lactate (tissue hypoperfusion) points to sepsis.
Cardiogenic. An S3 and a very high BNP indicate ventricular volume overload and pump failure.
questions.rationale: All shock states cause inadequate tissue perfusion, but the cause guides treatment. Hypovolemic shock shows signs of empty vessels (flat neck veins); cardiogenic shock shows congestion (JVD, crackles, S3, high BNP); septic shock shows infection and vasodilation (fever, warm skin early, elevated lactate). Giving fluid helps hypovolemic and septic shock but can worsen cardiogenic shock.
questions.takeaway: Flat veins = hypovolemic; full veins + crackles = cardiogenic; infection + warm skin = septic.
questions.hintContent: Recall what happens to the neck veins and lungs when the problem is volume loss versus pump failure versus vasodilation.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the 'signature' cue in each row (neck veins, lung sounds, infection source) and match it to the underlying mechanism.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Blood Pressure · Pulse Pressure and MAP
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client arrives in the emergency department after a motor vehicle crash. BP is 96/80, HR 124, and the skin is cool and pale. Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: The client's pulse pressure is {0}, which is considered {1}. The mean arterial pressure (MAP) is approximately {2}. The pulse pressure most likely reflects {3}.

options: 16 mm Hg
48 mm Hg
80 mm Hg
176 mm Hg
widened
normal
narrowed
64 mm Hg
72 mm Hg
85 mm Hg
88 mm Hg
increased intracranial pressure
reduced stroke volume with compensatory vasoconstriction
stiff, noncompliant arteries
aortic valve regurgitation

questions.rationale: Pulse pressure = SBP − DBP = 96 − 80 = 16 mm Hg (normal about 30–50), so it is narrowed. MAP = (SBP + 2 × DBP) ÷ 3 = (96 + 160) ÷ 3 ≈ 85 mm Hg. After trauma, blood loss reduces stroke volume (lowering systolic pressure) while sympathetic vasoconstriction maintains diastolic pressure — a narrowing pulse pressure is an early sign of hypovolemic shock, even when MAP is still adequate. Widened pulse pressure occurs with increased ICP, stiff arteries, and aortic regurgitation.
questions.takeaway: Narrow pulse pressure + tachycardia after trauma = early hypovolemic shock, even with an 'okay' MAP.
questions.hintContent: Recall the formulas for pulse pressure and MAP and what raises or lowers each side of the pulse pressure.
questions.hintStrategy: Do the math first (subtract, then weight the diastolic twice), then match the mechanism to the clinical context.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Peripheral Assessment · Ankle-Brachial Index
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: Refer to the Diagnostic Results for a client who reports right calf cramping when walking. Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: The right ankle-brachial index is {0}, which indicates {1}. The left ankle-brachial index of 0.92 is {2}.

options: noncompressible arteries
normal arterial flow
moderate peripheral artery disease
critical limb ischemia
normal
borderline
consistent with severe disease

questions.rationale: The ABI uses the higher ankle pressure on each side divided by the higher brachial pressure of both arms. Right: 92 ÷ 142 = 0.65. Using the right brachial (92 ÷ 138 = 0.67) or the lower ankle pressure (88 ÷ 142 = 0.62) are common errors. Interpretation: 1.00–1.40 normal, 0.91–0.99 borderline, ≤0.90 PAD (0.70–0.90 mild, 0.40–0.69 moderate, <0.40 severe), >1.40 noncompressible. The left ABI (130 ÷ 142 = 0.92) is borderline.
questions.takeaway: ABI = higher ankle ÷ higher arm (of both arms); 0.40–0.69 = moderate PAD.
questions.hintContent: Recall which ankle and which brachial pressure are used in the ABI calculation and the interpretation ranges.
questions.hintStrategy: Pick the correct numerator and denominator before dividing; distractor values come from choosing the wrong pressures.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: 0800: 80-year-old client with heart failure and atrial fibrillation takes digoxin 0.125 mg daily and furosemide 40 mg twice daily. Reports nausea, poor appetite for 3 days, and "yellow-green halos around lights." Apical pulse 54, irregular. BP 112/68. Lungs clear; trace ankle edema.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes and Laboratory Results. Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: The client's findings are most consistent with {0}. The client's {1} increases the risk for this condition. The nurse should first {2}.

options: an exacerbation of heart failure
digoxin toxicity
viral gastroenteritis
hypercalcemia
hypokalemia
blood pressure
trace ankle edema
furosemide dosing time
give the digoxin with food to reduce nausea
request an increase in the digoxin dose
withhold the digoxin and notify the provider
give the morning furosemide dose early

questions.rationale: Anorexia, nausea, visual disturbances (yellow-green halos), bradycardia, and a digoxin level above range indicate digoxin toxicity. Hypokalemia from the loop diuretic increases digoxin binding to the myocardium and increases toxicity; reduced renal function in an older adult also decreases digoxin clearance. The nurse withholds the digoxin and notifies the provider, who may order potassium replacement, ECG monitoring, and (for severe toxicity) digoxin immune fab.
questions.takeaway: Loop diuretic + digoxin: low K⁺ → toxicity (GI, visual, bradycardia) — hold and call.
questions.hintContent: Recall the classic signs of digoxin toxicity and which electrolyte imbalance potentiates it.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the condition from the cluster of symptoms and the drug level, then choose the risk factor and the safest first action that fit that condition.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: 1320: 61-year-old client with poorly controlled hypertension reports sudden, severe "tearing" pain between the shoulder blades that began 30 minutes ago. Diaphoretic and anxious. Radial pulse weaker on the left than the right.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes and Vital Signs. Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: The nurse recognizes that the client's findings are most consistent with {0}. The difference in arm pressures suggests {1}. The nurse anticipates an IV {2} to reduce heart rate and BP, with a target systolic BP below {3} within the first hour.

options: pulmonary embolism
acute myocardial infarction
acute aortic dissection
musculoskeletal strain
a cuff that is too small on the right arm
a dissection limiting blood flow into one subclavian artery
a normal variation between arms
an auscultatory gap in the left arm
thrombolytic
beta-blocker such as esmolol
vasopressor such as norepinephrine
rapid crystalloid bolus
100 mm Hg
120 mm Hg
160 mm Hg
180 mm Hg

questions.rationale: Sudden, severe, tearing or ripping chest or back pain in a hypertensive client, with unequal arm pulses or pressures (a difference >20 mm Hg), strongly suggests acute aortic dissection. Blood entering the aortic wall can compromise branch vessels such as the subclavian artery. Treatment begins with an IV beta-blocker (e.g., esmolol or labetalol) to lower heart rate and shear stress, then vasodilators if needed, targeting SBP <120 mm Hg within the first hour (2025 AHA/ACC). Thrombolytics are contraindicated and could be fatal.
questions.takeaway: Tearing back pain + unequal arm BPs = dissection: beta-blocker first, SBP <120 in the first hour, no thrombolytics.
questions.hintContent: Recall the classic presentation of aortic dissection and why heart rate control precedes vasodilation.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the condition from the pain quality and the unequal arm findings, then choose options consistent with reducing stress on the aortic wall.
